title: Rafi’ (ra) and Rifa’a (ra): Healed With the Prophet’s ﷺ Saliva | The Firsts | Dr. Omar Suleiman
description:
Before the Prophet ﷺ ever reached Medina, the Qur’an had already arrived there. Rafi’ ibn Malik (ra), one of six men from Yathrib who accepted Islam at Hajj, could read and write. The Prophet ﷺ gave him the written portions revealed up to Surah Yusuf, and his tribe, Banu Zurayq, became the first in Medina to hear the Qur’an recited in its masjid. He was killed at Uhud.

His son Rifa’a ibn Rafi’ (ra) fought at Badr, where an arrow struck his eye and the Prophet ﷺ healed it. His mother was the sister of ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites. Rifa’a went on to narrate the hadith of Jibril (as) on the rank of those who fought at Badr, and two well-known hadith about prayer: one about a man told three times to go back and pray, and one about a man whose words in prayer the angels raced to record.

title: The 12 Questions The Companions Asked The Prophet ﷺ | Anchored Ep. 5 | Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy
description:
Some hadith are hard to read and understand the first time around. 

One of them is the authentic narration in Bukhari and Muslim where the Prophet ﷺ says, “I was commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah.” Read alone, it can sound like an order of endless war against non-Muslims. The scholars who explained it read it a different way. In this hadith, “the people” refers to the pagan Arab tribes who broke treaty after treaty at the end of the Prophet’s ﷺ mission, not to all of humanity. The Qur’an sets peace as the default (“if they incline to peace, incline to it as well”). The Prophet ﷺ made treaties with non-Muslims and lived beside them in Medina. He also said to leave the Abyssinians and the Turks alone as long as they left the Muslims alone. In Islamic law, the justification for war is always protective.
